rawReadingSequence: Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-50
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A cartel coordinates output restrictions and higher prices. A prisoner's dilemma arises when each firm benefits from undercutting regardless of its rival's action, yet mutual undercutting leaves both worse off than cooperation.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare a firm's payoffs separately for each possible rival action.
Undercutting is dominant if it pays more in both comparisons.
Check whether mutual undercutting pays less than mutual cooperation.
WATCH OUT
A jointly profitable agreement may be unstable when each firm can gain by breaking it. Compare individual incentives, not just the sum of payoffs.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INDIVIDUAL INCENTIVES VERSUS JOINT GAINS

If Column keeps the agreement, Row gets 8 by undercutting rather than 6 by keeping it. If Column undercuts, Row gets 3 rather than 2 by undercutting. Column faces the same incentives. Both undercut and receive 3 each, although keeping the agreement would give 6 each. Individual incentives can undermine a mutually beneficial agreement.
CHECK YOURSELF
If the other firm keeps the agreement, why is a one-time promise to keep it vulnerable to undercutting?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
